title: AI Trained Only on Landscapes Confirms M87 Black Hole Ring, Settling 2022 Debate
excerpt: M87 black hole image confirmation: CSIRO’s GenDIReCT AI, trained only on landscape photographs and never on astronomical data, independently recovered the same 42-microarcsecond ring from Event Horizon Telescope data, matching the 2019 EHT measurement within 0.5% and countering a 2022 challenge
content:
When the Event Horizon Telescope produced the world's first image of a black hole in 2019, it carried an inherent limitation: the same team that collected the data was responsible for processing it. Now, a four-person team at Australia's national science agency has used an artificial intelligence system that had never encountered a black hole to independently verify the image's core feature — and the AI came back with the same answer.

The result, published in Nature November 11 under the title "Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*," features lead author Dr. Samuel Lai and colleagues at CSIRO. The paper carries the DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9.

"The fact that a system trained entirely on everyday photographs of the natural world can recover the same measurement as the most sophisticated radio telescope array humanity has ever built is a remarkable validation," said Dr. Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, the paper's corresponding author and a researcher at CSIRO's Space and Astronomy division. "We did not design this system to look for rings. We did not train it on radio data. It found what physics predicts."

Why Confirmation Matters

The EHT's April 2019 image of M87*, the supermassive black hole at the center of galaxy Messier 87, was a landmark achievement — but it also carried a structural vulnerability. Very Long Baseline Interferometry radio imaging requires station-based phase calibration: each antenna in the array must have its local phase errors corrected before data from all eight telescopes can be coherently combined. That calibration process depends on assumptions, and those assumptions are products of the same researchers who built and operated the array.

In 2022, Makoto Miyoshi, an assistant professor at Japan's National Astronomical Observatory (NAOJ), published a reanalysis of EHT data using different methods. His team argued that the ring structure visible in the 2019 image was likely an artifact of the array's sparse coverage and sampling bias rather than a genuine astrophysical feature. The paper generated significant discussion within the astronomy community and prompted multiple formal responses from EHT scientists.

How GenDIReCT Approaches the Problem

The CSIRO team's approach sidesteps calibration entirely. GenDIReCT — Generative Deep learning Image Reconstruction with Closure Terms — uses a latent diffusion model, the same class of architecture that powers many recent commercial image generators, but feeds it a different kind of observational data: closure phases and closure amplitudes.

These quantities, known as closure invariants, are formed by combining measurements from triangles and quadrilaterals of telescope baselines rather than individual stations. Because they are computed from ratios and differences across multiple antennae, any error that is local to a single telescope — antenna pointing drift, atmospheric delay, receiver noise — cancels out mathematically. The result is a set of observables that are immune to station-based phase errors, the very class of errors that the Miyoshi group argued could have contaminated the EHT image.

GenDIReCT's diffusion model was trained not on radio astronomy data but on natural photographs: landscapes, animals, objects. By learning the statistical structure of natural images at a fundamental level and then conditioning its output on the closure-invariant observables from the EHT dataset, it recovers a spatial image consistent with those observables without ever having been shown what a black hole is supposed to look like.

The Controversy It Addresses

The Miyoshi 2022 paper was not the first challenge to the EHT image, nor was it the last. Several independent groups published responses using different reconstruction methods, closure-based analyses, and additional observational constraints. One of them — published as Carilli and Thyagarajan 2022 — listed Thyagarajan as co-author and directly addressed the sampling-bias claims using closure phases. The CSIRO paper is the first to bring a generative AI system trained on no astronomical prior knowledge into the verification effort.

"The question being asked is a genuinely important one," said Dr. Laurent Loinard, EHT project director at Mexico's National Autonomous University's Institute of Radio Astronomy and Astrophysics, who was not involved in the research, describing it as "a remarkable piece of work." "Independent confirmation using fundamentally different methods is exactly how science is supposed to work."

What GenDIReCT Found

Given the full public EHT observational dataset — the same measurements that produced the original image — GenDIReCT recovered a ring with an angular diameter of 42.0 ± 0.2 microarcseconds. The EHT's own best-fit measurement from 2019 was 42 ± 3 microarcseconds. The match is within 0.5% of the EHT's central value and falls well inside the EHT's own uncertainty range.

What it reconstructed was the ring. GenDIReCT produced no alternative structures — no jet, no multiple rings, no ambiguous off-center blob — consistent with astrophysical models of a black hole shadow. The methodology was described in a prior paper in Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia, published in November 2025, establishing GenDIReCT's theoretical framework before the M87 application.

Why "No Prior Knowledge" Matters

The absence of astronomical training data is not an oversight; it is the system's primary epistemological strength. Any AI trained on existing black hole images, simulations, or radio interferometry data would carry the implicit assumptions embedded in that training corpus. If those assumptions are wrong — if the EHT reconstruction community has converged on a subtly biased set of priors — then a system trained on their outputs cannot serve as a genuinely independent check.

GenDIReCT's training corpus — natural landscape photographs — has no structural relationship to radio interferometry or astrophysics. Its "knowledge" of images is entirely statistical: it knows what natural scenes look like at a distributional level. When conditioned on the EHT closure-phase data, it is asking a question the training data has no stake in: what spatial structure is consistent with these calibration-independent observables? The answer it found was a ring.

The closure-invariant approach also addresses a subtler criticism of the Miyoshi analysis. Critics of the 2022 paper noted that Miyoshi's alternative reconstruction methods made their own assumptions about the data, particularly regarding the spatial frequency coverage of the array. GenDIReCT's closure-based input bypasses this debate by discarding precisely the data that is most sensitive to sparse-coverage artifacts.

Reactions from the Broader Community

The Nature paper has drawn commentary from several groups who had previously worked on the EHT verification problem. The result has been described as a meaningful addition to the evidence base, though researchers have noted it does not by itself resolve every open question about the M87* system, including details of the jet structure and the dynamics of the accretion flow.

Thyagarajan acknowledged the limitations directly. "This is a confirmation of the ring's existence and diameter," he said. "It is not a full characterization of M87*. The EHT collaboration has much more work ahead of it, and so do we."

Wider Applications

The closure-invariant framework is not unique to black hole imaging. The same mathematical structure appears in seismic tomography, where energy waves travel through the Earth's interior and their arrival-time differences at multiple stations form natural closure constraints; in medical computed tomography; and in atmospheric science, where multiply-scattered light creates observable closure-phase analogs.

Earlier CSIRO work published in 2026 applied the technique to Centaurus A, one of the closest radio galaxies to Earth and home to one of the most powerful known jets emanating from a black hole, and to 3C 279, a highly variable quasar roughly 5.3 billion light-years away whose jet appears to rotate in real-time observations.

A 2025 benchmarking study called InverseBench explicitly listed black hole imaging alongside seismology, optical tomography, and fluid dynamics as five canonical scientific domains for evaluating diffusion-based priors. The CSIRO team's result now provides an in-situ validation point for one of those domains.

What Comes Next

The next-generation Event Horizon Telescope is currently under development, with the goal of extending the original eight-station array to as many as 30 stations worldwide, including the first telescope on the Antarctic plateau. The expanded array will provide substantially denser coverage of the spatial frequency plane — the gap in that coverage was at the heart of the Miyoshi critique — and will make it possible to image the M87* ring with enough resolution to track structural changes over time.

The engineering contract for new antennas was signed with Germany's mtex technology GmbH in 2023, with delivery of prototype hardware scheduled ahead of a first ngEHT science campaign. CSIRO has indicated that GenDIReCT will be applied to ngEHT data as it becomes available.

For now, the finding stands as the most rigorous independent confirmation yet produced of the black hole shadow that made headlines in 2019 — derived by a system that, until it was given the EHT data, had never been asked to look at one.

The paper "Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*" appears in Nature Volume 659, pages 317–323, published November 11, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9

Frequently Asked Questions

What is GenDIReCT?

GenDIReCT — Generative Deep learning Image Reconstruction with Closure Terms — is an imaging technique developed by researchers at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency. It combines a latent diffusion model (the same class of AI architecture used in modern image generators) with closure invariants: mathematical observables derived from triangles of telescope baselines that are immune to the station-level calibration errors affecting conventional radio interferometric imaging. By training on ordinary photographs of natural scenes rather than astronomical data, GenDIReCT brings no prior assumptions about black holes to its reconstructions, making it genuinely independent of the original EHT team's methods.

Why was the EHT's 2019 black hole image controversial?

The 2019 EHT image of M87* was widely celebrated, but it carried a structural vulnerability: the team that collected the data was also responsible for calibrating and reconstructing it. Station-based phase calibration — the correction of local errors at each antenna — depends on assumptions that are part of the EHT's own methodology. In 2022, a team led by Makoto Miyoshi at NAOJ published a reanalysis arguing that the ring structure could be an artifact of the array's sparse spatial-frequency coverage and calibration choices. That challenge prompted formal responses from EHT scientists and motivated the search for genuinely independent confirmation methods.

How does GenDIReCT's confirmation differ from EHT's original imaging?

The EHT produced its image using standard VLBI calibration, which corrects for antenna-based phase errors before combining data from multiple telescopes. GenDIReCT never performs that calibration step. Instead, it works directly from closure phases and closure amplitudes — quantities formed from combinations of three or four baselines simultaneously, which are mathematically guaranteed to be free of any single-station errors. Its underlying diffusion model was trained on landscapes, animals, and everyday objects, not radio interferometry data. The match between GenDIReCT's recovered ring (42.0 ± 0.2 microarcseconds) and the EHT's original measurement (42 ± 3 microarcseconds) is therefore not a circular check: it is a structurally independent reconstruction using different mathematics and no shared assumptions.

What are closure phases in radio astronomy?

A closure phase is an observable formed by summing the measured phase differences between three telescopes connected as a triangle of baselines. Because atmospheric turbulence and electronic noise affect each antenna individually, any such local error cancels when you add up the three pairwise phase measurements around the triangle — a property Jennison first described in 1958. Closure phases therefore preserve genuine source structure while being insensitive to station-based calibration errors, making them the most reliable class of observables for VLBI reconstruction. GenDIReCT uses both closure phases (from baseline triangles) and closure amplitudes (from baseline quadrilaterals) as its sole inputs.

What is the next-generation Event Horizon Telescope (ngEHT)?

The ngEHT is a planned expansion of the existing EHT array from eight stations to as many as 30 worldwide, including the first telescope on the Antarctic plateau. The expanded network will provide far denser spatial-frequency coverage than the current array, closing the sampling gaps that the Miyoshi group argued could introduce reconstruction artifacts. The Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian is leading the expansion; the engineering contract for new antenna hardware was signed with Germany's mtex technology GmbH in 2023. CSIRO has stated it intends to apply GenDIReCT to ngEHT data as it becomes available.
